lessons.title: Earthquakes in Contrasting Wealth: Nepal & New Zealand

before.content_html:
Why Compare Two Earthquakes?

Earthquakes happen all over the world, but their effects are not the same in every place. The same magnitude shake can kill a hundred thousand in one country and barely a dozen in another. To understand why, geographers compare two earthquakes in places of very different wealth: Nepal in 2015 (a low-income country) and Christchurch, New Zealand in 2011 (a high-income country). The contrast tells us how money, planning and infrastructure shape the human cost of a hazard.

Nepal, 25 April 2015

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck just before midday, with its epicentre about 80 km north-west of the capital Kathmandu. It happened where the Indian Plate is being driven into the Eurasian Plate — the same collision that built the Himalayas. The shaking lasted around fifty seconds and triggered avalanches on Mount Everest.

Primary effects were severe. Around 9,000 people were killed and 23,000 injured. Around 600,000 buildings collapsed or were badly damaged, including UNESCO heritage temples in Kathmandu's Durbar Square. Roads and water pipes broke. Secondary effects followed. Avalanches killed 19 climbers on Everest. Nearly 8 million people were affected, with three million made homeless. Outbreaks of cholera and dysentery spread in displaced-person camps. The economy lost an estimated $7 billion — about a third of Nepal's GDP.

Key Fact

Nepal 2015: magnitude 7.8, around 9,000 dead, 600,000 buildings destroyed, 3 million made homeless, $7 billion in damage — roughly a third of Nepal's GDP.

Responses in Nepal

Immediate responses were dominated by international aid because Nepal's own emergency services were quickly overwhelmed. Search-and-rescue teams flew in from India, China, the UK and the US. The UN, Red Cross and Oxfam supplied tents, food, clean water and medical care. Helicopters were the only way to reach mountainous villages where roads were blocked.

Long-term responses have been slower. Donors pledged $4.1 billion at a Kathmandu conference, but bureaucratic delays meant that two years later most rural homes were still not rebuilt. The government has worked with the World Bank to set new earthquake-resistant building standards, but enforcement is uneven in remote areas.

Christchurch, 22 February 2011

A magnitude 6.3 earthquake struck Christchurch at lunchtime. It was an aftershock of a larger 7.1 quake five months earlier. The epicentre was just 10 km from the city centre and only 5 km deep, which made the shaking unusually violent for its size. New Zealand sits where the Pacific and Australian plates meet at a complex boundary, and Christchurch sits near a previously unknown fault line.

Primary effects: 185 people died, around half in the collapse of a single six-storey building (the CTV building). Around 100,000 buildings were damaged. The Anglican cathedral lost its tower. Liquefaction — where ground water turns wet sand into a liquid — ruined large areas of suburban Christchurch.

Secondary effects included an estimated $40 billion in damage and major disruption to the city for years. Many businesses left the central business district permanently. But the death toll, given the magnitude and location, was relatively low.

Key Fact

Christchurch 2011: magnitude 6.3, 185 dead, $40 billion damage. Far lower death toll than Nepal because of strict building codes, fast emergency response, public education and an experienced civil defence service.

Responses in Christchurch

Immediate responses were rapid and well-organised. New Zealand's Civil Defence response began within minutes. Search-and-rescue teams were on site quickly, supported by international teams from Australia, the US and the UK. Hospitals coped with the casualties. Power was restored to most of the city within five days.

Long-term responses included the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA), set up to coordinate the rebuild. The central business district was demolished and rebuilt to higher seismic standards. New Zealand reviewed and tightened its building code, and the experience strengthened earthquake education in schools.

Nepal's earthquake was much larger (7.8 vs 6.3 — about a hundred times more energy released). Yet its death rate was tens of times higher only partly because of the size. The bigger reason was building quality: brick and mud-mortar construction collapsed; reinforced concrete and timber-frame buildings designed to flex did not. Wealth doesn't change the geology, but it changes everything about how people meet the geology.

New Zealand introduced earthquake-resistant building standards after the 1931 Hawke's Bay earthquake. Steel frames, base isolators (rubber pads under buildings that absorb shaking) and reinforced concrete were the norm in modern construction. The CTV building, which killed 115 of the 185 victims, had been built in the 1980s but later investigation found design flaws — a reminder that codes only work when they are enforced and inspected.

Side-by-Side Comparison

The two earthquakes show that wealth changes outcomes more than magnitude does. Both were powerful, both struck near major cities, both caused billions in damage. But Nepal's death toll was around fifty times larger, despite a population that is only about five times larger than Christchurch's. The difference lies in resilience — the capacity to absorb shocks and bounce back.

lessons.title: Reducing Tectonic Risk: Monitoring, Prediction, Protection, Planning

before.content_html:
Managing Tectonic Hazards: The Four Ps

No country can stop an earthquake or an eruption. What we can do is reduce the human cost. Geographers group risk-reduction strategies under four headings: monitoring, prediction, protection and planning. They are sometimes called the four Ps. Each one targets a different part of the disaster cycle — before, during and after the event.

Monitoring

Monitoring means watching for warning signs. Volcanoes can be monitored using seismometers (to detect tremors caused by rising magma), GPS sensors (to spot ground bulging) and gas sniffers (sulphur dioxide rises before an eruption). The Hawaiian Volcano Observatory has detected and tracked dozens of eruptions, allowing people to leave on time. Earthquakes are harder to monitor in advance, but stress measurements along faults and changes in groundwater levels are studied. Earthquakes still strike with little warning, which is why monitoring is much more useful for volcanoes than for quakes.

Key Fact

Volcanoes are monitored using seismometers (small tremors signal rising magma), GPS sensors (ground bulges as magma fills the chamber) and gas sniffers (sulphur dioxide rises before an eruption).

Prediction

Prediction goes beyond watching — it tries to forecast when and where. Volcanic eruptions can sometimes be predicted hours or days in advance from a combination of seismic activity, gas readings and ground deformation. The 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland was predicted accurately enough that nearby farms were evacuated. Earthquake prediction is much harder. No reliable method exists for predicting the day, hour or street where an earthquake will strike. The best science can do is give probabilities — for example, 'there is a 60% chance of a magnitude 6+ earthquake in the San Francisco Bay Area in the next 30 years.' That kind of forecast is useful for planners but does not warn individuals.

Japan's system doesn't predict earthquakes hours in advance — it gives seconds. Sensors detect the fast-moving but harmless P-waves of a quake, calculate the size, and send alerts to phones, trains and factories before the slower, destructive S-waves arrive. Even ten seconds is enough to stop a bullet train, shut off gas mains and warn people to take cover. It saved hundreds of lives in the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake.

Protection

Protection is the strongest tool in the kit. It means designing buildings, infrastructure and defences that can withstand the hazard.

  • Earthquake-resistant buildings. Reinforced concrete frames, steel cross-bracing and base isolators (rubber-and-steel pads that let buildings sway) absorb shaking. Tokyo's skyscrapers can flex by several metres in an earthquake without falling.
  • Lava barriers and trenches. Around Mount Etna in Sicily, concrete barriers have been built to divert lava away from villages. They cannot stop the eruption but they can save homes.
  • Tsunami sea walls. Japan's coastline is lined with concrete walls up to 12 metres high. They saved lives in 2011, although the Fukushima wave overtopped them.
  • Strong public buildings. Schools, hospitals and police stations are built to higher seismic standards than ordinary homes, so they can act as refuges and continue functioning after a disaster.

Planning

Planning is what saves lives in the moments and hours after the hazard hits. Hazard maps identify which areas are likely to be flooded by tsunami, buried by lava or shaken hardest. Local authorities use them to decide what to build where. Evacuation routes are signposted in volcanic and tsunami zones. Japan runs nationwide earthquake drills every September; in California, schools practise 'drop, cover, hold on' regularly. Emergency-services rehearsals, well-stocked supplies and clear chains of command turn what could be a chaotic scramble into a co-ordinated response.

Key Fact

The four Ps work together. Monitoring gathers data, prediction interprets it, protection makes places stronger, and planning prepares people. Remove any one and the others become weaker.

A hazard map colour-codes danger zones — red for highest risk, yellow for moderate, green for low. Insurance companies use them to set premiums; planners use them to decide where to allow new schools and hospitals; residents use them to plan escape routes. Iceland's volcano hazard maps cover every active system.

Why HICs Manage Better Than LICs

High-income countries can afford the technology, the building codes and the trained services. Japan invests billions in tsunami walls; New Zealand drills its schoolchildren; Iceland tracks every volcano in real time. Low-income countries face a harder choice. Money spent on hazard management is money not spent on health, education or roads. International aid programmes (such as those run by the UN and World Bank) help, but the gap remains. The lesson is that risk reduction is not just a science problem — it is a development problem.

before.content_html:
The Global Atmospheric Engine

The world's weather is not random. It is driven by the way the atmosphere circulates between the equator and the poles. The Sun heats the equator more strongly than the poles, and this temperature difference sets the air in motion. Geographers describe this with the global atmospheric circulation model. It explains why the equator is hot and wet, why the Sahara and Australian deserts sit at the same latitudes, and why the UK is windy and changeable.

Pressure Belts and Cells

The model splits the atmosphere into three giant circulation cells in each hemisphere. At the equator, hot air rises. As it rises it cools and releases moisture, producing the heavy rainfall of the rainforest belt. This is a zone of low pressure. The risen air spreads polewards and sinks again at around 30° north and south. Sinking air warms and dries, creating the world's high pressure deserts — the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts all sit on this belt. Air then either flows back to the equator (the trade winds) or polewards to around 60°, where it meets cold polar air, rises again, and produces another belt of low pressure and stormy weather. The UK sits on this belt — which is why our weather is so unpredictable.

Key Fact

Air rises at the equator (low pressure, rainforest) and at 60° (low pressure, UK weather). Air sinks at 30° (high pressure, deserts) and at the poles (high pressure, polar deserts).

Tropical Storms: Where and When

Tropical storms have several names depending on where they form: hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific, typhoons in the western Pacific, and cyclones in the Indian Ocean. They all form between 5° and 30° north and south of the equator — never on the equator itself, because the spin needed to rotate the storm only exists away from it. The peak season is late summer in each hemisphere, when ocean temperatures are highest. Most form between June and November in the northern hemisphere.

How a Tropical Storm Forms

Several conditions must come together for a storm to develop. The ocean must be at least 26.5°C, and warm to a depth of about 50 metres — this provides the energy. The air must be unstable so that it rises easily, and there must be enough Coriolis effect to set the storm spinning — this is why storms form away from the equator. Wind speeds must also be similar from sea level upwards, otherwise the storm gets sheared apart before it can organise.

When all these conditions align, warm moist air rises rapidly off the ocean surface. As it rises it cools, and the water vapour condenses into clouds — releasing huge amounts of latent heat. This heat warms the surrounding air, causing it to rise faster, drawing in more warm air from the sea below. The Coriolis effect bends the inflowing air into a spiral. The storm is born.

The eye of the storm is a calm, clear column at the centre, around 30–65 km wide, where air is descending. Around the eye is the eye wall — a ring of towering thunderstorms with the strongest winds and heaviest rain. Outside the eye wall, spiral rain bands stretch hundreds of kilometres. The whole system can be over 1,000 km across, but the most violent activity is concentrated in the eye wall.

Climate Change and Tropical Storms

Climate change is heating the oceans, and warmer water means more energy available to fuel storms. Most scientists agree on three changes for a warmer world: more intense tropical storms (higher wind speeds, more rain), storms reaching higher latitudes (places like New York and Lisbon may face threats they have not faced before), and longer storm seasons. Whether the total number of storms is increasing is less certain — some research suggests fewer but stronger storms.

Key Fact

Tropical storms need ocean water above 26.5°C, low wind shear, and the Coriolis effect away from the equator. Climate change makes storms more intense, longer-lived and capable of reaching higher latitudes.

The Coriolis effect is what makes storms spin. It only works when an object is moving across latitudes — on the equator itself, the deflection is zero. Without Coriolis, low-pressure systems can grow but they cannot organise into a rotating storm. That is why hurricanes appear at 10–30° north or south but never directly on the line.
before.exam_tip_html: Examiners want the formation conditions stated in order: warm ocean (26.5°C), low wind shear, Coriolis effect, unstable air. For 6-mark 'Suggest how climate change might affect tropical storms', use 'might' or 'could' — predictions are uncertain. Mention intensity, latitude range and season length.

lessons.title: Tropical Storm Effects & Management: Hurricane Ida

before.content_html:
Hurricane Ida: A Modern Atlantic Hurricane

In late August 2021, Hurricane Ida swept across the Caribbean and into the United States. It is one of the most useful case studies for the AQA specification because it shows the full life of a modern hurricane: rapid intensification over warm seas, primary destruction at landfall, secondary effects hundreds of miles inland, and a clear contrast between rich-country and poor-country impact.

Path and Intensification

Ida formed as a tropical depression near Jamaica on 26 August. It strengthened over warm Caribbean waters — sea-surface temperatures were around 30°C, well above the 26.5°C threshold. Within 36 hours it had intensified from a Category 1 to a Category 4 hurricane, with sustained winds of 240 km/h. It made landfall in Louisiana on 29 August, the same date that Hurricane Katrina had struck the same coast 16 years earlier.

Key Fact

Hurricane Ida made landfall in Louisiana on 29 August 2021 as a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 240 km/h, almost exactly 16 years after Katrina hit the same coast.

Primary Effects

The damage at landfall was enormous. A storm surge of around 4 metres flooded coastal communities in Louisiana. Around one million homes lost power. New Orleans went into total blackout for the first time since Katrina. Roofs were torn from buildings; trees were flattened across hundreds of square kilometres; oil platforms in the Gulf of Mexico were damaged. Around 30 people in Louisiana died as a direct result of the storm.

Secondary Effects: The Northeast Floods

As Ida moved inland it weakened to a tropical depression but still carried huge amounts of moisture. Days later, the remnants reached New York and New Jersey. Record-breaking rainfall fell — over 80 mm in an hour in Central Park, the most ever recorded. Flash floods filled basement flats in New York where dozens of people drowned, unable to escape. Subway stations flooded. The total death toll across all states reached around 100. Damage was estimated at $75 billion, making Ida one of the costliest US hurricanes on record.

A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture — about 7% more for every 1°C of warming. As Ida tracked north it met a stalled cold front over the north-east. The collision squeezed an enormous load of tropical moisture out of the storm in a few hours. Climate scientists pointed out that this kind of extreme rainfall is now several times more likely than it was a century ago.

Immediate Responses

Louisiana ordered mandatory evacuations from low-lying coastal parishes 24 hours before landfall. The National Guard deployed 5,000 soldiers, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) pre-positioned generators and food, and 25,000 utility workers were sent in to restore power. The President declared a major disaster, freeing federal funds. Hospitals worked through the storm; emergency shelters opened in schools and gymnasiums.

Long-Term Responses

Recovery in Louisiana took months. Power was restored to most areas within two weeks, but parts of New Orleans were dark for over a month. Federal disaster relief and private insurance paid out around $50 billion. New York City changed its rules: basement flats now require flood-proofing if they are to be legally rented out, and the subway has new flood barriers. The state also accelerated investment in stormwater infrastructure. The hurricane prompted serious debate in the US about whether building codes should be tightened in known flood zones.

Key Fact

The US had advance warning, mandatory evacuations, federal disaster funds and insurance pay-outs of $50 billion. In a low-income country, neither the warning nor the recovery would have moved that fast.

Reducing Tropical Storm Risk

As with tectonic hazards, four tools cut the risk: monitoring (satellites and aircraft track storms continuously), prediction (storm tracks are now forecast accurately three to five days in advance), protection (storm shutters, sea walls, building codes) and planning (evacuation routes, shelters, public education). Ida shows that even an HIC can be devastated — especially when storms hit areas that haven't planned for that level of rain.

Hurricanes are graded from Category 1 (winds 119–153 km/h) to Category 5 (over 252 km/h) on the Saffir-Simpson scale. The scale predicts wind damage; it does not predict storm-surge or rainfall flooding, which is often the biggest killer. A Category 4 storm like Ida can be devastating, but a slow-moving Category 1 can also drown a city if it dumps enough rain.

lessons.title: UK Weather Hazards: The Storm Desmond Floods

before.content_html:
UK Weather Hazards

The UK does not face hurricanes or volcanic eruptions, but it does experience a range of weather hazards. Storms, heavy rain, snow and ice, drought, heatwaves and strong winds all cause disruption every year. The UK's position on the boundary between cold polar air and warm tropical air — the polar front — gives it the changeable weather it is famous for. As the climate warms, several of these hazards are becoming more extreme.

Types of UK Weather Hazard

  • Wind storms. Atlantic depressions can bring 100 km/h winds to UK coasts. Storms are now formally named (e.g. Storm Eunice, Feb 2022, with gusts of 196 km/h on the Isle of Wight).
  • Heavy rain and flooding. Persistent low pressure can bring weeks of rain. The Cumbria floods of December 2015 and the winter floods of 2019–20 are recent examples.
  • Snow and ice. Cold continental air can bury parts of the UK. The 'Beast from the East' of 2018 dumped half a metre of snow and shut schools and motorways.
  • Heatwaves. The UK passed 40°C for the first time in July 2022. Wildfires broke out around London and railway tracks buckled.
  • Drought. The summer of 2022 was the driest since 1976; reservoirs fell to 50% and hosepipe bans covered most of England.
Key Fact

UK weather hazards include storms, floods, heatwaves, droughts and snow events. Recent extreme examples include Storm Eunice (Feb 2022, 196 km/h gusts) and the July 2022 heatwave (UK passed 40°C for the first time).

Case Study: Storm Desmond, December 2015

Storm Desmond was an Atlantic depression that struck the UK on 4–5 December 2015. Powered by a corridor of warm, moist air from the Atlantic — sometimes called an atmospheric river — it dumped extraordinary amounts of rain onto north-west England. Honister Pass in the Lake District recorded 341.4 mm of rain in 24 hours, then a UK record. Rivers in Cumbria, including the Eden and the Kent, burst their banks within hours.

Causes

Several factors made Desmond so extreme. Saturated ground: November had already been wet, so the soil could absorb little more. Steep relief: the Lake District's mountains forced the moist air upwards, intensifying rainfall (orographic rainfall). Atmospheric river: a narrow corridor of tropical moisture funnelled directly at the UK. Climate change: warmer Atlantic waters held more water vapour, raising rainfall totals by an estimated 40% compared to a pre-industrial Desmond.

The combination is what made the storm record-breaking. Storms with one or two of these factors happen most years. A storm with all four is something the UK has rarely seen before. As the climate continues to warm, atmospheric rivers carrying more moisture will become more frequent. Saturated ground in autumn will carry forward into winter rain events more often. Defences sized for 20th-century rainfall totals will be tested more regularly. The pattern is not abstract — it is being measured year by year by the Met Office. Storm Desmond is now studied as a textbook case of attribution science, where researchers measure how much human-driven climate change has shifted the odds of a specific extreme event.

Impacts

Around 5,200 homes were flooded across Cumbria and Lancashire. Bridges in Carlisle, Cockermouth and Pooley Bridge collapsed. The town of Carlisle was hit hardest — 2,200 properties flooded, including a hospital that had to be evacuated. Two people died directly. Total economic cost was estimated at over £500 million. The clean-up took months; some families were not back in their homes for over a year.

Cumbria had already flooded in 2009 (Storm Cockermouth) and flood defences had been raised after that event. Desmond's rainfall was so far above the 2009 totals that the new defences were overwhelmed. The lesson is that defences sized for past events can be undersized for a changing climate. Cumbria's defences have since been raised again, this time to take account of climate-change projections.

Responses

The Environment Agency issued severe flood warnings 24 hours before the worst rain. The Army was deployed to evacuate residents. Mountain rescue teams worked through the night. After the immediate emergency, the government provided £50 million in financial aid. The flood response prompted a major review of flood defences nationally, and Cumbria's defences were rebuilt to higher standards.

Key Fact

Storm Desmond's 341 mm of rain in 24 hours broke the UK record. Climate change is estimated to have boosted the rainfall by around 40%. UK weather extremes are becoming more frequent and more intense.

The Met Office records show: 9 of the 10 wettest years on record have happened since 2000; the UK passed 40°C for the first time in 2022; storm names ran out for the first time in 2015–16; and floods costing more than £100 million happen roughly twice as often as in the 1980s. The trends are not subtle.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK weather hazards include storms, floods, heatwaves, droughts and snow events — all becoming more extreme with climate change.
  • Storm Desmond (Dec 2015) brought 341 mm of rain in 24 hours to Cumbria, flooding 5,200 homes including a Carlisle hospital.
  • Met Office data confirms the UK climate is becoming more extreme: 9 of the 10 wettest years on record since 2000, plus the first 40°C reading in 2022.

Memorise: 341 mm rain at Honister Pass, 5,200 homes flooded, Carlisle's 2,200 properties, £500 million damage. For 9-mark 'evidence' questions, link multiple Met Office statistics into a coherent argument.

before.content_html:
The World's Most Biodiverse Biome

Tropical rainforests cover only 6% of the Earth's land surface but contain more than half of all species. They lie in a band on either side of the equator: the Amazon, the Congo, parts of South-East Asia and northern Australia. The climate is hot and wet all year. Average temperatures stay between 25°C and 30°C. Rainfall is over 2,000 mm a year, often falling daily in the afternoon. The lack of seasons means plants and animals can grow continuously.

Structure: The Four Layers

Tropical rainforests are layered like a multi-storey building. Each level has its own climate and species.

  • Emergent layer — tallest trees, up to 50 metres, breaking through the canopy. Strong winds and direct sunlight; harpy eagles nest here.
  • Canopy — the dense leafy roof, around 30–40 metres high. Most photosynthesis happens here, and most rainforest species live here. Howler monkeys, sloths and parrots feed in the canopy.
  • Understorey — smaller trees, shaded by the canopy. Plants have large leaves to capture what little light reaches them.
  • Forest floor — dim, humid, with thin soil. Decomposers work fast here, breaking down fallen leaves within weeks.
Key Fact

Rainforests have four layers: emergent (tallest, ~50 m), canopy (most species), understorey (shade), and forest floor (decomposers). Each supports different organisms.

Interdependence

In a rainforest, climate, plants, animals and soil all depend on each other. Hot, wet conditions support fast plant growth. Plants release water vapour through their leaves (transpiration), which forms clouds and falls as rain — meaning the forest creates much of its own rainfall. Animals pollinate plants and disperse their seeds. Decomposers recycle nutrients fast enough that the thin soil supports the world's tallest trees. Cut down enough trees and the cycle breaks — less transpiration means less rain, drier conditions, and the forest cannot regrow.

It seems counter-intuitive that the world's most productive ecosystem sits on poor soil. But because decomposition is so fast in the heat and humidity, nutrients don't accumulate — they are taken up by plants almost immediately. The forest holds most of its nutrients in living biomass, not the soil. This is also why slash-and-burn farming destroys rainforest fertility quickly: cut the trees, and the nutrients are gone.

Adaptations of Plants

Plants compete fiercely for light. Buttress roots spread sideways at the base of tall trees to support their height in shallow soil. Drip-tip leaves are pointed so that heavy rain runs off quickly — if water sat on leaves, mould would grow. Lianas are woody vines that climb other trees rather than growing their own thick trunks. Epiphytes — orchids, bromeliads — live on the branches of other trees, getting nutrients from rainwater and air. Some plants flower and fruit only once every few years to avoid being predictable to predators.

Adaptations of Animals

Animals are adapted to the layered environment. Howler monkeys have prehensile tails that work as a fifth limb in the canopy. Sloths move so slowly that algae grow in their fur, providing camouflage. Poison dart frogs are brightly coloured to warn predators of toxic skin. Toucans have huge bills to reach fruit on slender branches that wouldn't support their weight. Jaguars are the only big cat that hunts mainly in water.

Key Fact

Rainforest plants compete for light. Buttress roots support tall trees in thin soil; drip-tip leaves shed heavy rain; lianas climb others; epiphytes grow on branches; flowering can be unpredictable to outwit predators.

Issues of Biodiversity

Biodiversity in tropical rainforests is unmatched. The Amazon alone contains an estimated 16,000 tree species and 2.5 million insect species. This biodiversity has enormous value: 25% of modern medicines come from rainforest plants. The yew tree of the Amazon produced taxol, used to treat cancer. Many rainforest species have not yet been studied. Every hectare lost is a potential cure or food source disappearing forever. Lose biodiversity and the next pandemic, the next antibiotic, the next staple crop may be gone before we know it existed.

Up to 50% of the rainfall in the Amazon is recycled water that has passed through plants. Trees draw water from the soil and release it through their leaves; the water vapour rises, forms clouds and falls as rain hundreds of kilometres away. Recent research suggests forests act as a 'biotic pump', pulling moist air inland from the ocean. Cut the forest, and rainfall declines — not just locally but across continents.

The Amazon: A Case Study in Pressure

The Amazon Rainforest is the world's largest tropical rainforest, covering 5.5 million square kilometres — roughly twenty times the size of the United Kingdom. Around 60% of it lies in Brazil, with the rest spread across Peru, Colombia, Venezuela and other South American countries. It is home to about 30 million people, including 350 indigenous groups. The Amazon also stores around 100 billion tonnes of carbon — releasing it would equal a decade of global fossil-fuel emissions.

Rates of Deforestation

Since 1970, around 17% of the Amazon has been cleared. Rates have varied with politics and economics. They peaked in 2004 (around 27,000 km² in a single year), fell sharply in the 2010s as Brazil enforced new laws, then surged again under President Bolsonaro (2019–2022). They have begun falling again under President Lula since 2023. The total area lost is now about the size of France.

Causes of Deforestation

  • Cattle ranching is the biggest single driver. Around 80% of cleared Amazon land is now used for cattle, supplying beef to global markets.
  • Commercial agriculture, especially soya beans for animal feed, is the second largest. Brazilian soya is a global crop.
  • Logging, both legal and illegal, removes valuable hardwoods like mahogany. Illegal logging accounts for an estimated half of all timber leaving the Amazon.
  • Mineral extraction — gold, iron ore and bauxite — clears land and causes pollution. The Carajás iron mine in Brazil is one of the world's largest.
  • Road building, especially the Trans-Amazonian Highway, opens previously inaccessible rainforest to settlement and clearance.
  • Hydroelectric dams like the Belo Monte dam flood huge areas of forest.
  • Settlement and population growth, partly driven by Brazilian government schemes encouraging migration to the Amazon basin from poorer regions.
Key Fact

Cattle ranching is the biggest cause of Amazon deforestation, accounting for around 80% of cleared land. Soya farming for animal feed and logging follow.

Impacts

Economic impacts are mixed. Brazilian beef and soya exports earn billions of dollars and provide jobs. Mining provides government tax revenue. But the long-term costs are huge. Soil erosion: with no tree roots holding the soil, heavy rain washes the topsoil away, leaving land that cannot easily be farmed again. Climate change: deforestation contributes around 10% of global CO₂ emissions. Trees that once absorbed carbon now release it as they burn or rot. Water cycle disruption: less transpiration means less rainfall, both locally and across the continent. Biodiversity loss: countless species are pushed towards extinction. Indigenous communities lose their land, their culture and often their lives in conflicts with loggers and miners.

Climate scientists have warned of a 'tipping point' — a level of deforestation beyond which the Amazon cannot generate enough rainfall to sustain itself, and would convert to dry savannah. Current estimates put this point somewhere between 20% and 25% loss. As of 2024, around 17% has gone. The choice over the next decade is whether the Amazon survives as a forest or collapses as a system.

Sustainable Management Strategies

Sustainable management aims to use the rainforest without destroying it. Selective logging means harvesting only mature trees of certain species, leaving the rest of the forest intact. The Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certifies timber from properly managed forests. Replanting restores cleared areas. Conservation areas like national parks and biosphere reserves limit human activity. Education teaches local communities the long-term value of intact forest. Ecotourism brings in income from visitors who want to see the rainforest, providing an economic alternative to logging or mining.

International Action

Several international tools target rainforest protection. International agreements like CITES restrict trade in protected species and certified hardwoods. Debt-for-nature swaps see wealthy nations cancel a country's foreign debt in return for protecting forest land. Brazil has used this tool with several creditor countries. Carbon-credit schemes pay countries to keep forests standing, since intact forests absorb CO₂. Critics argue that policing all this from outside is hard, and that the only sustainable solution is to support the people who live in and around the rainforest financially.

Key Fact

Sustainable Amazon management combines selective logging, replanting, conservation areas, ecotourism and international tools like debt-for-nature swaps and carbon credits.

The Amazon is vast, remote and crossed by few roads. Many areas are days from the nearest police post. Loggers and miners often have political backing. Brazil's government uses satellite monitoring (called DETER) to spot new clearings, but acting on that data on the ground is slow. The fundamental challenge is that local people often need the income that deforestation provides — without alternative livelihoods, enforcement alone cannot succeed.

What Is Desertification?

Desertification is the process by which fertile land turns into desert. It does not mean sand dunes invading farmland; rather, it means soil losing its productivity until crops will no longer grow. Around 12 million hectares of land are lost to desertification every year — an area larger than England. The places most at risk are semi-arid regions on the fringes of existing deserts, where rainfall is already low and unreliable.

The Sahel: Africa's Front Line

The Sahel is a band of dry grassland running across Africa just south of the Sahara, from Senegal in the west to Sudan in the east. Around 100 million people live there. Rainfall averages 100–600 mm a year and is highly seasonal — so a single bad rainy season can devastate harvests. The Sahel has been desertifying for decades, and the population has tripled since 1960, increasing pressure on the land.

Key Fact

The Sahel is a semi-arid belt across Africa, south of the Sahara, with 100 million people and 100–600 mm of rain a year. It has been desertifying for decades.

Causes of Desertification

Desertification has several interlocking causes — climate change driving the trend, and human activity making it worse on the ground.

  • Climate change. Rising temperatures increase evaporation. Rainfall patterns are shifting; some Sahel regions have seen 25% less rain than in the 1950s.
  • Population growth. More people means more food needed, more cattle, more firewood, more pressure on the same land.
  • Removal of fuelwood. Trees are felled for cooking and heating fuel. Without their roots, soil washes or blows away.
  • Overgrazing. Too many cattle or goats strip vegetation faster than it can regrow.
  • Over-cultivation. Farming the same field continuously without rest exhausts the soil's nutrients.
  • Soil erosion. When vegetation is gone, wind and rain remove the topsoil, sometimes in a single dust storm.

Desertification is rarely caused by one thing. A drought makes farmers move their cattle further; the cattle overgraze the new area; vegetation thins; the soil loses its grip; the next storm washes the topsoil away; the land can no longer support the cattle, so the farmers move again, repeating the cycle. Each step makes the next one worse. Climate change is now adding background pressure to a system already under strain.

Reducing the Risk

Solutions target both the land and the people who farm it. Strategies fall into four broad groups.

  • Water and soil management. Magic stones (lines of stones along contours) trap rainwater and let it soak in. Mulching with crop residues holds moisture in soil. Bunds (low earth banks) slow runoff.
  • Tree planting. Roots bind soil. Trees shade crops and reduce evaporation. The most ambitious project is the Great Green Wall (see below).
  • Appropriate technology. Locally-made drip-irrigation, fuel-efficient stoves (using less wood) and treadle pumps for water make farming sustainable without expensive equipment.
  • Rotation and reduced livestock. Letting fields rest, rotating crops, reducing herd sizes — all give the land a chance to recover.
Key Fact

Desertification can be reduced through water and soil management (mulching, bunds), tree planting (Great Green Wall), appropriate technology (drip irrigation, efficient stoves) and reduced grazing pressure.

The Great Green Wall

The Great Green Wall is a flagship African Union project. The plan: plant a 7,000-kilometre belt of trees and vegetation right across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti, to halt the southward spread of the Sahara. Launched in 2007, it has been complicated. Some early plantings failed because the wrong species were used. Progress is uneven across the 11 participating countries. By 2024, only around 18% of the planned area had been restored, but the project has shifted approach — now focusing on a 'mosaic' of tree planting, soil restoration and farm land management rather than a single continuous line of forest. It is now estimated that fully delivering the Wall would create 10 million jobs and lock up 250 million tonnes of carbon.

Scale, funding and conflict have all slowed it down. Trees planted in the wrong soil at the wrong time die quickly. Funds promised by donors have not always arrived. Local conflict in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger has made some areas dangerous to work in. Crucially, the project depends on local farmers, not international planters — and farmers need to see real benefit from the trees (firewood, fodder, soil improvement) to maintain them.

before.content_html:
Two Kinds of Wave

All coastal change starts with the wave. Waves are formed when wind blows across the sea surface, dragging energy from the air into the water. The distance the wind blows over — the fetch — controls how big the wave gets. Atlantic-facing UK coasts like Cornwall and Pembrokeshire have a fetch of thousands of kilometres, so they receive much bigger waves than sheltered North Sea coasts.

Geographers split waves into two types. Destructive waves are tall, steep and frequent (10–14 per minute). Their backwash — the water rushing back down the beach — is more powerful than their swash, so they drag sand and shingle away from the coast. Constructive waves are lower, longer and less frequent (6–8 per minute). Their swash beats their backwash, so they push material up the beach and build it. Storm conditions favour destructive waves; calm weather favours constructive waves.

Key Fact

Destructive waves are tall, steep and frequent (10–14 per minute) with strong backwash that erodes. Constructive waves are low, long and less frequent (6–8 per minute) with strong swash that builds beaches.

Weathering at the Coast

Before waves can erode a cliff, weathering often weakens the rock first. Weathering happens before any material is moved. Two types matter at the UK coast. Mechanical weathering includes freeze–thaw: water seeps into cracks, freezes overnight, expands by 9% and prises the rock apart. The chalk cliffs of the South Downs lose chunks each winter this way. Chemical weathering includes carbonation: rainwater absorbs CO₂ and forms a weak carbonic acid that slowly dissolves limestone and chalk, widening cracks and joints.

Mass Movement

Once weathered, weakened cliff material falls under gravity. This is mass movement. There are three forms to know:

  • Sliding — rock and soil slip down a flat surface in a single block, usually after heavy rain saturates the ground.
  • Slumping — saturated soft cliffs (like the boulder clay of Holderness) rotate downwards along a curved surface, leaving a stepped cliff face. Slumping is the dominant process on East Yorkshire's coast.
  • Rock falls — chunks of rock break off vertical or near-vertical cliffs and tumble to the beach. Common on the chalk cliffs at Beachy Head.

Wave Erosion

Destructive waves erode the coast in four ways:

Hydraulic power. Waves slam into a cliff and force air into cracks at high pressure. As the wave retreats the trapped air expands explosively, prising the rock apart. This is the dominant process during storms on hard-rock coasts.

Abrasion (sometimes called corrasion). Waves pick up sand, pebbles and rocks and hurl them at the cliff base, sandpapering it away. You can see abrasion's smoothed, polished base on most UK sea cliffs.

Attrition. The pebbles and rocks already in the water knock against each other, slowly becoming smaller, smoother and rounder. Attrition does not erode the cliff — it shapes the sediment that eventually becomes beach material.

Solution (corrosion). Slightly acidic seawater dissolves alkaline rock such as limestone and chalk. Slow but steady — it widens joints and helps caves form.

Transportation: Longshore Drift

Eroded sediment doesn't stay still. The most important transport process at the UK coast is longshore drift. Waves usually approach the beach at an angle (driven by the prevailing wind), so their swash carries sand up the beach diagonally. Gravity then pulls the backwash straight back down the slope. The result is a zigzag movement of sediment along the coast, often hundreds of metres a year.

On the Holderness coast, longshore drift moves sediment southwards from Flamborough Head towards Spurn Head at around 1.5 metres per day. On the south coast of England, sediment moves eastwards along the English Channel. Where this drift is interrupted by a structure such as a groyne or harbour wall, sand piles up on one side and the beach shrinks on the other.

Key Fact

Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast in a zigzag pattern. The swash arrives at an angle (set by the prevailing wind), the backwash returns straight down the slope. Net movement on UK east and south coasts is southwards or eastwards.

Deposition

Waves drop their sediment when they no longer have the energy to carry it. Deposition happens where the water is sheltered (inside a bay, behind a headland, or in a river estuary), where waves are constructive, or where transport is interrupted (against a groyne, for example). Sand is dropped first as it is finest; pebbles and shingle are dropped where wave energy is higher.

UK beaches change shape with the seasons. In summer, calm conditions and constructive waves rebuild the beach — sand and shingle are pushed up to form a high berm. In winter, frequent Atlantic storms send destructive waves that drag material back offshore, lowering the beach profile and exposing the cliff base to attack. The same beach can look completely different in July and January. Coastal managers use this to time soft engineering: beach nourishment is usually done in spring, before summer's natural rebuild begins.

Why Coastlines Look the Way They Do

UK coasts are not built randomly. They are the product of two things working together — the underlying geological structure and the four wave-erosion processes from the previous lesson. Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the sea at right angles (a discordant coast), the soft bands erode faster, leaving the hard bands sticking out as headlands. Swanage Bay in Dorset is the classic example. Where the rock runs parallel to the sea (a concordant coast), the coast looks straight and uniform.

Erosion Landforms

Once a discordant coast forms headlands and bays, erosion attacks the headlands themselves. The sequence of landforms is one of the most-tested topics in the course, so learn it as a chain.

1. Crack. Hydraulic power and abrasion exploit a vertical weakness or joint in the headland. Over decades the crack widens.

2. Cave. Continued erosion enlarges the crack into a cave at the base of the cliff, undercutting the rock above.

3. Arch. When two caves meet through the headland, or a cave breaks through the back of the headland, an arch is formed. Durdle Door in Dorset is a textbook example.

4. Stack. Erosion thins the arch's roof until it collapses, leaving an isolated pillar of rock standing offshore. Old Harry Rocks at the eastern end of Studland Bay show this stage.

5. Stump. Wave action eventually wears the stack down to a low rump visible only at low tide.

Cliffs and Wave-Cut Platforms

Cliffs retreat by a slightly different process. Waves attack the base of the cliff, cutting a wave-cut notch. With the base undermined, the rock above eventually collapses under gravity. The cliff line steps backwards, and the flat surface left at the base of each cliff retreat becomes a wave-cut platform. The platforms at Hunstanton in Norfolk and at Robin Hood's Bay in North Yorkshire show neat striations of bedded rock.

Key Fact

The erosion sequence on a headland is: crack → cave → arch → stack → stump. UK examples: Durdle Door (arch) and Old Harry Rocks (stack), both Dorset.

Deposition Landforms: Beaches

When waves no longer have the energy to carry sediment, they drop it — usually inside a sheltered bay between two headlands. The result is a beach. Sandy beaches form where wave energy is low (e.g. Bournemouth, with constructive waves and fine river-supplied sand). Pebble beaches form where wave energy is higher (e.g. Brighton, where larger material is dropped first). Beaches are dynamic — they are the same beach in summer and winter, but their profile changes dramatically with the season.

Sand Dunes

Where there is plenty of sand, a wide flat beach exposed at low tide and a steady onshore wind, sand can be blown landwards and trapped by vegetation to form sand dunes. The youngest dunes (embryo dunes) sit closest to the sea; older, more vegetated dunes (yellow dunes, then grey dunes) form further inland. Studland Bay in Dorset and Formby in Lancashire are good UK examples.

Spits and Bars

When longshore drift carries sediment along a coast and the coast suddenly changes direction (for example at a river mouth), the sediment keeps moving in its original direction. It builds out into the sea as a long, narrow ridge of sand and shingle — a spit. The end of the spit is often curved (a recurved end), shaped by waves arriving from a different direction during storms. Behind the spit, sheltered water collects mud and silt and a salt marsh develops.

Spurn Head, at the southern end of the Holderness coast, is the textbook UK example. Sediment eroded from cliffs further north is carried south by longshore drift and dropped where the Humber Estuary opens. Spurn extends nearly 5 km into the estuary; salt marsh has developed in its lee. If a spit grows right across a bay or river mouth and joins the land on the other side, it is called a bar. Slapton Sands in Devon and Chesil Beach in Dorset are bars.

Key Fact

Spurn Head is a 5 km spit at the south end of the Holderness coast, formed by longshore drift carrying eroded cliff material southwards. A salt marsh has developed in the sheltered water behind it.

Putting It Together: A UK Coastline

The Dorset coast in southern England is the classic UK case study. The discordant section between Studland and Swanage produces headlands (Old Harry Rocks) and bays (Studland, Swanage). Further west, hard bands run parallel to the sea (concordant), interrupted only where the sea has broken through to form the circular cove at Lulworth. Further west still, the long shingle ridge of Chesil Beach — an 18 km bar — protects the lagoon (the Fleet) behind it. Erosion landforms (Durdle Door arch) and deposition landforms (Chesil Beach bar) sit within walking distance of each other, all on the same stretch of coast.

In Dorset the resistant rock is Portland limestone and chalk; the weak rock is Wealden clay and Bagshot sand. The chalk forms vertical cliffs (Old Harry Rocks) because it is hard but jointed; the clay erodes back into bays (Swanage Bay) because it is much softer. Where the chalk runs along the coast (further west towards Lulworth), it forms long straight cliffs broken only where the sea has punched through to the softer rock behind. Geology, in short, is the master variable: it sets the speed, shape and direction of every landform you see.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Discordant coasts (rock at right angles to the sea) produce headlands and bays; concordant coasts (rock parallel to the sea) produce long straight cliffs.
  • The erosion sequence on a headland is crack → cave → arch → stack → stump — with Durdle Door and Old Harry Rocks as Dorset examples.
  • Deposition landforms include beaches, sand dunes, spits (Spurn Head, 5 km) and bars (Chesil Beach, 18 km), all formed where wave energy drops or longshore drift is interrupted.

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark 'Suggest' questions on landform formation, use a numbered sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4. Examiners look for the chain of cause and effect, not just labels. A stage with the wrong example loses marks; a stage without any example loses marks too.

For 9-mark 'Assess' questions on coastal management, examiners want a balanced argument with a clear judgement — not a list of strategies. lessons.title: Rivers: Long Profile, Cross Profile & Processes

before.content_html:
From Source to Mouth

Every river begins at a source — usually high ground where rainfall, snowmelt or a spring releases water. From there it flows downhill through a channel, joined by smaller streams (tributaries) at confluences, until it reaches its mouth at the sea or a lake. The total area of land drained by the river and its tributaries is called the drainage basin.

Geographers split the river into three sections: the upper course (close to the source, steep and narrow), the middle course (gentler gradient, wider valley) and the lower course (very gentle gradient, wide flat valley). The same river looks completely different in each section, because the dominant processes change as you move downstream.

The Long Profile

A long profile is a side-on diagram of the river from source to mouth. The line is steepest at the source (high gradient) and flattens out towards the mouth (low gradient), forming a smooth concave curve. The shape reflects how the river uses its energy: in the upper course energy fights friction with the rough bed and banks, so most goes into vertical erosion; further downstream the smoother channel needs less energy for friction, so the river can carry more water and a larger load with a much gentler slope.

The Cross Profile

The cross profile looks at the river from the side, slicing across the valley. The shape changes dramatically downstream:

Upper course. Narrow, steep-sided V-shaped valley. The channel itself is narrow and shallow, with a rough bed of large angular boulders. Vertical erosion dominates because the river is cutting down towards sea level. Interlocking spurs jut from alternate sides of the valley.

Middle course. Wider valley with gentler slopes. The channel is broader and deeper. Lateral (sideways) erosion becomes more important as the river starts to swing across its valley. Meanders begin to form.

Lower course. Very wide, almost flat valley. The channel is wide and deep but the gradient is tiny. Deposition dominates — the river drops the load it has carried downstream. Wide flood plains and levees develop.

Key Fact

Upper course = vertical erosion (V-shaped valley, interlocking spurs). Middle course = lateral erosion (meanders). Lower course = deposition (flood plain, levees, estuary).

Erosion Processes

Rivers erode in four ways — the same processes that operate at the coast, plus one more.

  • Hydraulic action. Fast-flowing water hits the bed and banks, forcing air into cracks and prising them apart. Most powerful in upland streams during floods.
  • Abrasion (corrasion). Sand and pebbles carried by the water scrape against the bed and banks, sandpapering them away. The dominant erosion process in most UK rivers.
  • Attrition. The pebbles in the water knock against each other, becoming smaller, smoother and rounder. Attrition shapes the load, not the bed.
  • Solution (corrosion). Slightly acidic river water dissolves alkaline rock such as limestone and chalk — slow but steady.

Erosion can also be split by direction. Vertical erosion deepens the channel and dominates in the upper course (helping form V-shaped valleys). Lateral erosion widens the channel by cutting sideways — dominant in the middle and lower courses, helping form meanders.

Transportation

A river carries its load in four ways:

  • Traction. Large boulders and pebbles roll along the bed. Only happens during floods when the river has the most energy.
  • Saltation. Smaller pebbles bounce along the bed in a series of hops, picked up briefly by the current and dropped again.
  • Suspension. Fine sand, silt and clay are held up in the water column. This is what makes rivers look brown after heavy rain.
  • Solution. Dissolved minerals, especially from limestone catchments, are carried invisibly in the water.

Deposition

Rivers deposit their load when they no longer have the energy to carry it. This happens when the river slows down — for example, when the gradient flattens, when the channel widens, when the river enters the sea, or after a flood when discharge drops. Larger material is dropped first (it needs more energy to carry); the finest particles travel furthest. This is why the upper course has angular boulders, the middle course rounded pebbles, and the lower course mud and silt.

Key Fact

Transport processes by particle size: traction (largest, rolled along the bed) → saltation (bounced) → suspension (held up in the water) → solution (dissolved). Bigger particles need more energy to move.

Discharge is the volume of water passing a point each second, measured in cubic metres per second (cumecs). It increases downstream as more tributaries join. The River Severn has a discharge of around 2 cumecs at its source on Plynlimon in mid-Wales but over 100 cumecs by the time it reaches Worcester — and over 600 cumecs during major floods. Higher discharge means more energy to erode and transport, which is why floods reshape rivers so dramatically.

before.content_html:
Why Each Course Has Its Own Landforms

Different parts of a river create different landforms because the dominant process is different. The upper course is shaped by vertical erosion (cutting down), the middle course by lateral erosion (cutting sideways), and the lower course by deposition (dropping the load). Examiners expect you to know one named UK example for the major landforms — learn the chain, then learn one place name for each.

Upper Course: Interlocking Spurs and Waterfalls

In the upper course the river has not got enough energy to cut sideways through the hills, so it weaves between them. The result is interlocking spurs — ridges that project from alternate sides of the valley, with the river snaking between them. The view down the valley looks like fingers interlocking from each side.

A waterfall forms where a band of hard rock lies over softer rock. The softer rock erodes faster, undercutting the hard rock above. The river falls vertically into a deep pool at the base — the plunge pool — which is itself eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion. Over thousands of years the hard rock above eventually collapses without support, and the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep narrow gorge behind it.

1. A river crosses a band of hard rock lying over softer rock.

2. The softer rock is eroded faster, leaving the hard rock as an overhanging step.

3. The river plunges over the step. Hydraulic action and abrasion erode a deep plunge pool at the base.

4. The plunge pool undercuts the hard cap rock, which eventually collapses without support.

5. The waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep, narrow gorge of recession behind it. High Force on the River Tees in County Durham is a clear UK example.

Key Fact

High Force on the River Tees is a 21 m waterfall where the hard Whin Sill rock lies over softer limestone. The plunge pool below is over 6 m deep. The waterfall has retreated upstream, leaving a 700 m gorge.

Middle Course: Meanders and Ox-Bow Lakes

Once the gradient flattens, the river starts swinging from side to side. The result is a meander. On the outer bank the water flows fastest because the channel is deeper there; this energy erodes the bank into a steep river cliff. On the inner bank the water flows slowly because the channel is shallow; the river drops material here, building a gentle slip-off slope of sand and shingle.

Over time the meander becomes more and more curved as erosion deepens the outer bend and deposition builds the inner one. Eventually two outer bends erode towards each other; during a flood the river cuts across the narrow neck between them. The new straighter channel takes over and the abandoned meander loop becomes an ox-bow lake. Ox-bow lakes are common on the lower River Severn near Worcester, and on the River Cuckmere in East Sussex.

Lower Course: Flood Plains, Levees and Estuaries

Near the mouth, the river spreads out across a wide flat valley. When the river floods, water spreads beyond the channel. As it does so it slows down, and the coarsest material is dropped first — right next to the channel. Over hundreds of floods this builds levees — raised natural banks that line the river. Beyond the levees, the floodwater drops finer silt across the wider flood plain, creating fertile farmland.

At the mouth the river meets the sea and slows further still. If the tide is strong it forms a wide estuary — the lower Severn, Thames and Humber are good UK examples. The fresh and salt water mix; mudflats and salt marsh develop along the banks. Estuaries are vital ports (Liverpool, Bristol, Hull) and important wildlife habitats.

1. Lateral erosion deepens the outer bends of two neighbouring meanders, and deposition builds up the inner bends.

2. The neck of land between the two meanders becomes narrower over time.

3. During a flood the river has the energy to cut straight across the narrow neck.

4. The new shorter channel takes over; deposition seals off the old meander loop.

5. The abandoned curve becomes an ox-bow lake, gradually drying out as silt fills it in.

Key Fact

On a meander, water flows fastest on the outer bend, eroding it into a steep river cliff. On the inner bend the water is slow, so material is deposited as a gentle slip-off slope.

A Worked UK Example: The River Tees

The Tees rises in the Pennines and flows 137 km to the North Sea at Middlesbrough. In its upper course on Cross Fell it shows interlocking spurs and the High Force waterfall. In its middle course near Yarm it loops in textbook meanders. Near its mouth it widens into a large estuary lined with industrial complexes. One river demonstrates almost every fluvial landform in the course, which is why exam questions sometimes ask for landforms 'along' a named UK river.
before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark 'landform formation' questions, structure your answer as a numbered sequence with cause and effect at each stage. Examiners reward sequential logic over a list of features. Always include a UK named example: High Force for waterfalls, the lower Severn for ox-bow lakes, the lower Tees for an estuary. Stages without examples lose the place-detail marks; examples without stages lose the process marks.

before.content_html:
When a River Floods

A river floods when its discharge exceeds the capacity of its channel and water spills over onto the surrounding land. Flooding is a natural process — healthy rivers flood roughly every couple of years, depositing fertile silt across the flood plain. The problem comes when people build homes, farms, schools and infrastructure on those flood plains. UK floods now cost the economy over £1 billion in an average year, and the cost is rising as the climate warms.

Storm Hydrographs

A storm hydrograph shows how a river's discharge responds to a single storm. It plots rainfall as bars on one axis and river discharge as a line on the other, both against time. Several features matter:

Peak rainfall. The highest rainfall recorded during the storm.

Peak discharge. The highest river discharge recorded after the storm. The peak comes some time after the rain because water takes time to reach the river.

Lag time. The time gap between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Short lag time = water reaches the river quickly = high flood risk. Long lag time = water reaches the river slowly = lower flood risk.

Rising limb. The line of the graph as discharge climbs. A steep rising limb means water is reaching the river fast.

Falling limb. The line as discharge drops back to normal. A gentle falling limb means the channel is draining slowly — flood risk persists.

Key Fact

A short lag time, steep rising limb and high peak discharge all signal a flashy hydrograph — a drainage basin where water reaches the river fast. This is high flood risk. Urban basins, basins with impermeable rock and steep relief all produce flashy hydrographs.

Physical Factors That Increase Flood Risk

Four physical factors control how quickly water reaches the river after rain:

  • Precipitation. Heavy or prolonged rainfall is the most obvious cause. Cumbria's flooding in December 2015 saw 341 mm of rain in 24 hours — far more than any drainage basin can absorb. Snowmelt during a sudden thaw can also produce huge flood discharges.
  • Geology. Impermeable rocks like granite and clay force water to run off the surface rather than soaking in. Permeable rocks like chalk and limestone allow water to soak in, slowing the runoff and reducing flood risk.
  • Relief. Steep slopes mean water runs off quickly. Upland UK basins like the Cumbrian Lakes have very steep relief and short lag times. Flat lowland basins like the Cambridgeshire Fens have long lag times.
  • Saturation. When the ground is already wet from previous rain, it cannot absorb more — so all new rainfall runs straight off. November and December storms in the UK are often the most dangerous for this reason.

Human Factors That Increase Flood Risk

People can change a drainage basin's response to rainfall almost as much as the natural factors themselves.

  • Urbanisation. Concrete, tarmac and roof tiles are impermeable. Rain that fell on grass or soil now flows straight off into drains, then into the river. Urban basins like the lower Thames have very flashy hydrographs. New housing on flood plains makes this worse.
  • Deforestation. Trees absorb water through their roots and slow runoff. When woodland is cleared for farming or development, water reaches the river faster.
  • Farming practices. Heavy machinery compacts soil; ploughing in autumn leaves bare fields exposed to winter rain; livestock paths channel runoff downslope. All increase how fast water reaches the river.
  • Climate change. Warmer Atlantic waters hold more moisture, which means heavier rainfall events. The Met Office records show 9 of the 10 wettest UK years on record have happened since 2000. The frequency of major UK floods has roughly doubled compared to the 1980s.
Key Fact

Urbanisation increases flood risk in three ways: impermeable surfaces (concrete, tarmac, roofs) stop infiltration; storm drains carry water to the river much faster than natural flow; new housing on flood plains puts more property at risk.

Comparing Two UK Drainage Basins

The differences are starkest when you compare two basins side by side. The upper Eden in Cumbria has steep relief, impermeable slate and shale, high winter rainfall, and is rural with sheep grazing. Its hydrograph is flashy: short lag time, steep rising limb, very high peak. The upper Thames in Oxfordshire has gentle relief, much permeable chalk, lower rainfall and a mix of farmland and small towns. Its hydrograph is much smoother: longer lag time, gentle rising limb, lower peak. The Eden floods every couple of winters; the upper Thames much less often.

Three trends are pushing UK flood risk steadily upwards. First, climate change is making rainfall events more intense; the Met Office estimates Storm Desmond's rainfall was around 40% heavier than a similar storm a century ago. Second, ageing flood defences are not always re-sized for current conditions; some defences were built for once-in-100-year events that now happen every 25. Third, more building on flood plains has put roughly 5.2 million UK properties at risk — one in six homes. The combination is why floods that used to make headlines once a decade now happen most winters.
